input: text1 and text2 are ASCII lowercase strings of lengths n and m; empty strings are accepted and min(n,m)+1 fits the collection bound. Collections are ordinary finite dense arrays/lists, not subclasses, proxies, sparse/accessor-backed collections. Strings are ordinary/primitive strings. Every collection length and computed allocation size fits [0,4294967295], with padded sizes explicitly included. No concurrent mutation or built-in monkey-patching is allowed. Preconditions are not runtime-checked, and allocation/resource capacity or completion is not guaranteed by declared bounds. JavaScript integer inputs are primitive safe-integer Number, excluding negative zero, NaN, infinities, fractions and BigInt.
return: Length of a longest sequence appearing in both strings in the same order, not necessarily contiguously.
mutation_aliasing: Inputs and caller-held aliases remain unchanged; only private working state is used. The Solution instance retains no state.
numeric: Every DP entry is in [0,min(n,m)]. The saved diagonal preserves the prior-row/prior-column dependency before an in-place row update. ASCII restricts both languages to identical character units. All integer inputs/intermediates remain within [-9007199254740991,9007199254740991]; no bitwise coercion is used.
complexity: O(n*m + 1) time, with O(1) early return when either string is empty, and O(min(n,m)+1) auxiliary space. The shorter string controls the rolling row. Bounds include ordinary built-in operations/allocations and assume bounded-word arithmetic, constant-time indexing, amortized append/pop and any explicitly stated hash/sort behavior.
source_accounting: The complete standalone source is 698 UTF-8 bytes, including every helper, Solution wrapper, signature, loop, built-in call, annotation/comment, whitespace and terminal newline. Helpers are fully charged per candidate, not free shared libraries. No imports, runtime-generated implementations or hidden source expansion are used. Any eventual judge-interface adapter is additional charged source.
